sentences.text: Almost every new idea is built upon the work of those who came before.
Some people argue that in any field, it is impossible to make a significant contribution without first being strongly influenced by past achievements.
I largely agree that the past shapes new work, but I believe the word impossible claims too much.

sections.role: Body 1 — How the past shapes new work

sentences.text: First, past achievements really do shape almost every important contribution.
We learn from earlier work what has already been tried and what still needs solving.
For example, a scientist must understand existing theories before she can improve upon them.
This shows that knowledge of the past usually provides the foundation for new discovery.
Even bold new ideas often grow as a response to the work of earlier thinkers.
Without learning what came before, a person may simply repeat old mistakes.
To this extent, the influence of past achievements is genuinely important.
Second, however, the claim that contribution is impossible without such influence goes too far.
Certain people make important breakthroughs precisely because they are not bound by the past.
Consider a self-taught inventor who solves a problem in a way no expert had ever considered.
Such cases show that fresh, untrained thinking can sometimes lead to real contributions.
Strong influence from the past can even trap people in old assumptions and habits.
A few great advances have come from outsiders who knew little of the established field.
Past achievements usually help, then, but they are not always strictly necessary.
In conclusion, past achievements shape and support most significant contributions.
But it is not truly impossible to contribute without their strong influence.
Most progress builds on the past, yet fresh and independent minds can still break new ground.
